hints: Remember what an enthalpy change of formation arrow means in the cycle, formation of one mole of compound from its elements, so think about the direction of the arrows from the elements box to reactants and to products.

Recall the Hess Law expression for this route, sum of formation enthalpies of products minus sum for reactants, and check you multiply each value by its balanced equation coefficient before subtracting.
walkthrough:
Picture the Hess cycle correctly**
You have reactants going to products directly with $\Delta H_r$. The indirect route goes down from reactants to elements (the reverse of formation) then back up from elements to products (formation). That is why the maths always ends up as products minus reactants. The elements box is the common baseline at the bottom.

Add up with stoichiometry first**
Do not just add one of each value. The equation is $\text{K}_2\text{Cr}_2\text{O}_7 + 4\text{KCl} + 3\text{H}_2\text{SO}_4 \rightarrow 2\text{CrO}_2\text{Cl}_2 + 3\text{K}_2\text{SO}_4 + 3\text{H}_2\text{O}$. So for products: $$2(-580) + 3(-1438) + 3(-286) = -1160 - 4314 - 858 = -6332\ \text{kJ mol}^{-1}$$ For reactants: $$(-2061) + 4(-437) + 3(-814) = -2061 - 1748 - 2442 = -6251\ \text{kJ mol}^{-1}$$

Subtract to get the reaction enthalpy**
Now apply Hess Law: $$\Delta H_r = -6332 - (-6251) = -81\ \text{kJ mol}^{-1}$$ The negative sign shows the reaction is slightly exothermic. Keep the unit as $\text{kJ mol}^{-1}$ and the sign in your final answer.

Final answer: $\Delta H_r = \Sigma \Delta H_f^\ominus(\text{products}) - \Sigma \Delta H_f^\ominus(\text{reactants})$
$= [2(-580) + 3(-1438) + 3(-286)] - [(-2061) + 4(-437) + 3(-814)] = -81\ \text{kJ mol}^{-1}$

hints: Think about the octahedral shape of $[\text{Cr}(\text{NH}_3)_4\text{Cl}_2]^+$ with two identical $\text{Cl}$ ligands, how can the two $\text{Cl}$ ligands be arranged relative to each other, next to each other or opposite each other?
walkthrough:
See the two different geometries**
This is an octahedral complex of type $\text{MA}_4\text{B}_2$, with four $\text{NH}_3$ and two $\text{Cl}$ ligands around $\text{Cr}^{3+}$. The two $\text{Cl}$ ligands can sit at $90^\circ$ to each other on the same side, the cis isomer, or at $180^\circ$ opposite each other, the trans isomer. Different spatial arrangement with the same formula is cis-trans, also called geometrical, isomerism.

hints: Start from the isolated $\text{Cr}^{3+}$ ion, its five 3d orbitals are degenerate, then think what happens to that degeneracy when ligands approach in an octahedral arrangement.
Recall that colour in transition metal complexes is not emission, it comes from removing certain wavelengths from white light, so what electronic process absorbs that light?
Link the absorbed photon energy to the gap between the split d orbital sets, and think about what colour you actually see relative to what is absorbed.
Consider why cis and trans arrangements would split the d orbitals by a slightly different amount, even though the ligands are the same, and how that changes the absorbed wavelength.
walkthrough:
Split the d orbitals**
Free $\text{Cr}^{3+}$ is $3\text{d}^3$ with all five d orbitals at the same energy. When six ligands approach octahedrally, lone pairs repel d electrons unequally. Orbitals pointing directly at ligands are raised more than those pointing between ligands. So you get two sets, lower and higher, separated by a gap $\Delta E$. This splitting is the key to all transition metal colour.

Absorb light to jump the gap**
White light shines on the solution. If a photon has energy exactly equal to $\Delta E$, with $E = hf$, it can be absorbed to promote a d electron from the lower set to the higher set. This is a d-d transition. Only that specific wavelength is removed. The rest passes through or is reflected.

Understand what colour you see**
You never see the colour that is absorbed, you see what is left. For example, if red-yellow light is absorbed, the transmitted light looks green-violet. That is why we say the observed colour is complementary to the absorbed colour. Without partial d occupancy and splitting, as in $\text{Cr}^{3+}$, there would be no visible absorption and the complex would be colourless.

Explain why cis and trans differ**
Both isomers contain the same metal and same ligands, but $\text{NH}_3$ and $\text{Cl}^-$ have different field strengths. In the cis isomer the two $\text{Cl}$ ligands are $90^\circ$ apart, in the trans isomer they are $180^\circ$ apart. The repulsion pattern on the d orbitals is therefore slightly different, so $\Delta E$ is different. A different $\Delta E$ means a different frequency, $f = \Delta E/h$, is absorbed, so the complementary colour left for you to see is different, one green and one violet.

Final answer: In the octahedral complex the 3d orbitals are split into two energy levels of different energy.
An electron can be promoted from the lower d set to the higher d set by absorbing a photon of visible light (d-d transition).
The colour seen is the complementary colour to that absorbed.
The cis and trans isomers have different arrangements of ligands so the d-orbital splitting energy, $\Delta E$, is different, different frequencies of light are absorbed, giving different observed colours.
